<Ssyarua>
The large lake Talia tended to hang around was called Ssyarua, its name a slick and slippery and foreign sounding. Talia knew it was hard to pronounce and that was part of the reason she chose it. Talia herself rarely bothered to name things – names are cages, after all – but the elves and dryads who lived in her domain needed labels, symbols, something to clutch onto. So, Ssyarua it became, although it bore no deeper meaning than the simple fact Talia was amused at hearing how people might try and say it out loud.

Ssyarua was no ordinary lake after being under Talia's care for a few thousand years. It was as much a living entity as the flora and fauna Talia created and nurtured. The water shimmered with a strange inner glow, phosphorescent in shades of violet and green that pulsed faintly like a living thing. Beneath the surface, its depths teemed with serpentine fronds, swaying like hungry fingers reaching for a meal, along with bright coral-like growths dotting the bottom edges of the lake.

And then, there were the lily pads, if you could even call them that. They were giant, their surfaces large enough to support three or four men lying down. They varied from your typical lily color, with shades of dark green veined with purple that reflected brightly when the sun hit just right. They weren't plants in the traditional sense – their flesh felt more like damp leather, soft and pliable underfoot but think and strong and capable of locomotion.

These weren’t just typical idle flora. Talia had seeded these creations herself, sculpted them with the utmost care over decades, tweaking them here and there. The lily pads writhed slightly when anything disturbed their waters – be it fish, bird, or clumsy intruder – sending tendrils and runners creeping outward like octopus arms. Each pad was sentient in its own right, capable of "deciding" whether a being on its surface amused or annoyed it.

And woe to the unlucky soul who annoyed it.

Talia uses them to transport guests across the lake instead of boats. Talia doesn't allow any boats in the waters she controls, not even canoes.

Ssyarua was vast, but not endless, about seven miles wide at its broadest point, and stretching a little over twelve miles in its winding entirety. Its shores were surrounded by jungle thickets where the trees leaned out over the water, laden with fruit and flowers. The lake teemed with a wide variety of exotic life forms, from jewel-scaled fish schooling beneath the surface, wildly varied reptiles and amphibians, to massive carnivorous plants. Patches of crimson and black reeds stood tall near its shallows, snapping at passing insects like hungry eels. Above it all, winged creatures circled lazily in the humid air, some shaped like oversized dragonflies with metallic sheens, others utterly alien, like the creatures that looked like floating air jellyfish, paper thin and see-thru pink.
</Ssyarua>

Throughout her lands there are enchanted oracle pools that will draw people in, whispering in their mind, showing them visions of their future. To truly get a reading on the future, the recipient will need to immerse themselves naked in the pool. The spirits are bound to the pools by Talia, kept there for her amusement.

Aschar, the Smiling Ooze:

Aschar didn’t just live in the pool, it was the pool, kind of. Imagine a kid blowing bubbles in their milk, except it’s a primordial goo the color of bruises. Black and purple, shiny as oil slicks, eyes sliding in and out of its gelatinous mass like zits you can’t stop popping. Answers so full of double meanings you’re dizzy by the time it spits you out - if it spits you out. People said the way it spoke, it could sell water to a drowning man. Not that you’d need to be drowning for it to want you under.

Drellon, the Keeper of Smells:

Looks sort of like a massive shit golem. The air around Drellon’s pool stank like the world's most rotten fart. Rot and copper, heavy and sharp. Drellon stood by the edge like an abandoned scarecrow come to life, hunched and knotted, its skin draped in vines like something long dead propped up for show. But what really made your guts crawl were the bees. Wasps. Flies? Whatever was swarming its face, buzzing loud and angry, pouring out of holes where eyes should’ve been. The pool itself bubbled lazily, its edges ringed with jagged bones like teeth gnashing around its perimeter. People didn’t go to Drellon for fun, they went because they had no other choice. Its truths hit like blunt trauma, stripped bare of hope or comfort. Predictions? Unavoidable. Dire. And often fatal. The pool wasn't really water anymore but more of a shit filled quagmire.

Lyshina, the Bloom That Sees:

Lyshina was hot sex wrapped in petals and thorns. Her pool was surrounded by these gigantic flowers that oozed nectar so sweet it made your mouth water just standing there. The spirit herself? Imagine if a pin-up girl and a bouquet had a baby, then dunked her in bioluminescent glitter, eyes always glowing like little golden suns. She had hips swaying with petals that changed colors every time you blinked and lips that dripped words sticky as honey. Glowing flora adorned her hair, always shifting, growing, changing. Towering a hundred meters high above the surrounding canopy like it was trying to peek into whatever version of heaven Talia probably thought was overrated. Its bark wasn’t bark. Not exactly. It was flesh, not the kind of dry, dead stuff you’d expect, but smooth, taut, and pinkish, like the exposed skin inside a mouth.

Then there was the defining feature: the slit. The "entrance," if you could call it that, stretched down the middle of the Wombtree’s trunk, 5 meters high from the ground gaping slightly and glistening with sticky golden sap. Always dripping, always moist. It had a slight stink but it was the sort of stink that drew people in. It also oozed this viscous, orange, syrupy goo that caught the sunlight in strange ways, like dollar store glitter was trying to escape its prison of golden sludge. The sap had a smell, too. Something between raw honey and something much, much dirtier. You’d swear it tasted like every guilty pleasure you weren’t ready to admit to. Somewhere near the top of the slit, the Wombtree’s "clit" jutted out like a knot in the bark, swollen and gleaming under a constant veil of leaking nectar. Talia called it the "sugar button." Visitors had learned pretty fast that touching it was pretty effective at coaxing more of that vision-inducing goop. Stimulating the sugar button sent the Wombtree into overdrive. The slit would gush sap, and the bark would tremble, the leaves would shake, releasing thick waves of misty pollen that buzzed in your lungs like warm bees. It wasn’t a quick high, either. Whatever the tree pumped into you, it hit deep and stayed for hours. Made people laugh, cry, scream, cum, and sometimes all at once. For obvious reasons, elves and dryads spent a lot of time around the tree, somewhat addicted to the effects.

They called it the Spore Grove, but that was just because "Dick Shroom Forest" didn’t sound dignified enough when whispered around campfires or scrawled into maps. Perpetually covered by night, a mile-wide cluster of fungal stalks stretched skyward in a chaotic erection of biology, sprouting from the soft loam like gods were playing a cosmic prank on evolution. And of course not ALL mushrooms looked like dicks. 

Some were short and stubby, capped with bright, swollen domes that shimmered under the light like they’d been polished. Others rose taller than trees, veined stems wrapped in ridges and curves that suggested no one designed them by accident. Emeraldis. That’s what the elves called it, their shining crown perched high in the sprawling canopy of Talia’s jungle domain. It wasn’t just a city; it was a woven tapestry of elven society that reached to the treetops, where thick wooden bridges swung between gargantuan trunks. It was an ancient example of elven artistry and engineering born from the raw materials of the jungle. There was no stone here, no iron, no straight-edged architecture imposed on the land. 

Trees in Emeraldis towered hundreds of feet tall, trunks wide enough to carve out multiple homes without weakening their integrity. Elven huts and towers twisted organically out of the wood, their structures shaped rather than built, as though they’d grown themselves into perfectly curving arches and spirals. Rope bridges stretched across yawning gaps in the canopy, creaking gently with the weight of passing elves who moved with the nimbleness of dancers. At night, bioluminescent fungi embedded into the bark gave the entire city a ghostly glow, bathing the surroundings in a soft, pulsing light that made the jungle floor below seem like an abyss. Glowing elven lanters, fueled by magic, lit the city at night. Fire was not allowed here for obvious reasons. Cooking was performed by magic as well.

Talia allowed Emeraldis to exist. Not out of sentimentality, but because she enjoyed them and knew they valued the land as much as she did. These elves weren’t intruders, not like others. They didn’t plunder or demand control; they simply asked for sanctuary. Their small, quiet songs floated down from the canopy in ways that made the jungle itself seem more vibrant and alive. And Talia, crazy as she was, appreciated their flavor of existence. They entertained her with their long lives, endless stories, and fleeting dramas. The fact that they worshipped her, not overtly, not obnoxiously, but with deep respect for her chaos and her power, defnitely didn’t hurt.
